extracted.intended_audience: students of American government and politics
extracted.subtask_description: A college-level textbook chapter describing U.S. foreign policy doctrines, principles of international law, and the organization/administration of national defense (Army, Militia, Navy, and military bureaucracy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monroe Doctrine — non-colonization and non-intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: The American continents, by the free and independent condition which they have assumed and maintain, are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monroe's message (Dec. 1823) declared the U.S. would consider any attempt by European powers to extend their system to any portion of this hemisphere as dangerous to U.S. peace and safety; existing colonies/dependencies would not be interfered with, but governments which had declared and maintained independence would be protected against European interposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monroe Doctrine — opposition to forcible deprivation of self-government
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States will not permit any European country or combination of countries to forcibly deprive an American state of the right and power of self-government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As articulated by Secretary Olney (1895) and applied by President Cleveland; the U.S. will not relieve states from international law obligations nor prevent their enforcement, but opposes forcible interference with self-government and shaping of political destinies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monroe Doctrine — prohibition of territorial aggrandizement (Roosevelt 1901)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Monroe Doctrine declares that there must be no territorial aggrandizement by any non-American power at the expense of any American power on American soil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: President Roosevelt clarified the doctrine: the U.S. does not guarantee a state against punishment for misconduct provided such punishment does not take the form of acquisition of territory by a non‑American power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roosevelt Corollary — U.S. responsibility to preserve order
rubrics_metrics.description: If a nation shows that it knows how to act with decency in industrial and political matters, keeping order and paying obligations, it need fear no U.S. interference; brutal wrongdoing or impotence may finally require intervention by a civilized nation, and in the western hemisphere the U.S. cannot ignore its duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roosevelt's 1904 corollary to the Monroe Doctrine implies the U.S. may intervene in Latin-American countries to preserve order and prevent European intervention; Taft echoed concerns about preventing perpetuation of irresponsible government or escape from obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: International law as part of domestic law
rubrics_metrics.description: International law is part of our law and must be ascertained and administered by domestic courts whenever questions depending upon it are presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there is no treaty or controlling executive/legislative act or judicial decision, courts must resort to customs and usages of civilized nations and to works of jurists as evidence; international law comprises treaties, statutes, judicial doctrines, authoritative writers, and recognized practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects of the law of peace (international law topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: International law (law of peace) defines what constitutes an independent state; fundamental rights and duties of states; methods by which new states come into existence and are recognized; character and acquisition of state property; territorial waters; diplomatic privileges and immunities; jurisdiction over aliens; piracy; conditions for interference in other states; expatriation and naturalization; treaty-making and abrogation; arbitration and mediation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These topics form the substantive content of peaceful international relations and are to be learned from treaties, statutes, court decisions, official documents and authoritative writers; variation exists between nations' legists and courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of war topics
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of war governs declaration of war, non-combatants, privateering, prisoners of war and their treatment, instruments of war and bombardment of towns, use of explosives, effect of war on property of belligerent states and neutrals, military occupation effects on property, rights and duties of neutrals, contraband, blockade, right of search, and prize courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules regulate the conduct of hostilities and are derived from treaties, practices, and judicial decisions; textbook notes the existence of accepted rules even though legists may disagree on particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: International arbitration and permanent court of arbitration
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations may submit controversies to arbitration; the Hague conferences recommended permanent arrangements including a court of arbitration composed of up to four persons from each country selected for recognized competence in international law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. and other powers concluded arbitration treaties to submit questions not affecting national independence or honor; examples include the Alabama Claims tribunal (Geneva) which rendered a damages award to the U.S.; Hague conferences (1899, 1907) recommended inquiry commissions and permanent arbitral institutions though they did not establish compulsory arbitration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional power to raise and support armies (constitutional limit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress enjoys an unlimited power to raise and support armies, subject to the constitutional requirement that military appropriations shall not be for a longer term than two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this power Congress organizes the Army and Militia by statute, fixing maximum numbers, terms of service, ranks and structural details; actual in-service numbers are determined by the President within statutory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular Army organization and statutory limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Army is organized under acts of Congress which provide maximum numbers of men and officers, terms of service, ranks and grades, strengths of regiments and divisions, and other system details; law fixed total enlisted strength at not more than 100,000 men (historical statutory example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The President determines the number in actual service subject to statutory caps; the text gives historical composition (regiments of cavalry, artillery, infantry, etc.) as illustrative of statutory organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlistment terms and reserve liability (Regular Army)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volunteers enlist for a term of seven years — the first four years in active service with the colors and three years in the reserve army — liable to call at any time (Law of August 24, 1912).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory term creates an active/reserve structure and reserve liability for mobilization; example drawn from early 20th-century law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia/National Guard statutory classification and membership ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Congressional authority to organize, arm, and discipline the militia, laws (Jan. 21, 1903 and May 27, 1908) declare all able-bodied citizens between ages eighteen and forty-five to be members of the militia, divided into organized militia (National Guard) and the Reserve Militia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enlistment in the National Guard is voluntary; many join for social reasons; ordinary citizens may be in the Reserve Militia without active knowledge; federal law integrates state forces for national service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal integration and training of the National Guard
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal statutes authorize the Secretary of War to issue military stores to state organized militia and arrange for their participation in maneuvers and field practice with the regular army; federal officers attend encampments and joint exercises are encouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 1903/1908 legislation seeks to make state militia more immediately serviceable in time of need by federal supervision, drills, and participation with regular troops, reducing confusion and delays at the outbreak of hostilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential authority to call out the militia (exclusive judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the President deems it necessary to execute the laws of the Union, suppress insurrections, or repel invasions, he may call out such number of the militia as he deems necessary; the authority to decide whether an exigency has arisen belongs exclusively to the President and his decision is conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Martin v. Mott and commentary by Justice Story: this places large discretionary power in the President's hands but implies corresponding responsibility; statutory basis and judicial recognition make the presidential determination final upon others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts-martial jurisdiction and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts-martial belong to the executive department, are not part of the federal judiciary, and are not limited by grand jury/ jury-trial provisions; their sentences, if legally convened and within authorized punishments, are not alterable by civil courts; but if a court-martial lacks jurisdiction over the subject-matter or inflicts a punishment forbidden by law, civil courts may inquire and give redress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military law enforcement is vested in special military courts to preserve discipline; civil courts will not interfere with valid courts-martial decisions but will review jurisdictional defects or illegal punishments (citation: Dynes v. Hoover).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval establishment and enlistment requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional power exists to 'provide and maintain a navy' consisting of ships of war, officers, enlisted men, docks and navy-yards; term of service in the U.S. Navy is four years; applicants for enlistment must be American citizens, able to read and write English, and take the oath of allegiance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The navy's vessels are distributed among Atlantic, Pacific, and Asiatic fleets; historical personnel numbers are given; immigration and language/citizenship standards are used to reduce aliens in the service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military administration: duties of Secretary of War and staff organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War (appointed by President with Senate advice/consent) directs military establishments, fortifications, rivers and harbors, bridges, supervises administration of insular affairs (e.g., Philippines), construction of the Panama Canal, military education, and must examine all estimates of appropriations and expenditures for the War Department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine duties are delegated to an assistant secretary and chief clerk; a network of chiefs (adjutant-general, inspector-general, quartermaster-general, surgeon-general, chief of engineers, chief of ordnance, chief signal officer, judge-advocate-general, etc.) administer records, inspection, supplies, medical services, construction, legal affairs and insular administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Staff creation and rotation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress created a General Staff (act of Feb. 14, 1903) composed of officers detailed from the army under rules prescribed by the President; officers may serve on the General Staff for only four years at most, and on returning to the army must remain there at least two years before re-detailing except in time of emergency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The General Staff includes general officers and field-grade officers to provide directing points of contact with the rank and file; the Chief of the Staff acts under the direction of the President and Secretary of War.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of special volunteers and drafting in wartime
rubrics_metrics.description: In war the Army has been composed of special volunteers called into service under presidential proclamation and acts of Congress; in long wars beyond the strength of the regular army and organized militia, special volunteers would likely be again employed and drafting may be resorted to as in the Civil War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, volunteers and citizen soldiers played major roles (e.g., volunteers of 1861–65); the organized militia/National Guard reduces need for immediate volunteer calls but extended conflicts still may require volunteers/draft.
